explain.say: Now see the tongue. Your mouth has tiny nerve sensors that warn you when food is too hot, above about 43 degrees. Capsaicin fits onto those same sensors, like a key in a lock, and switches them on, even though nothing is hot. Sneaky, right?

faq.a: Capsaicin is the oily chemical in chillies that makes them taste hot. Most of it is in the pale ribs inside the chilli, near the seeds.

faq.q: Why does chilli feel hot if it isn't hot?
faq.a: Capsaicin switches on the nerve sensors in your mouth that normally detect heat above about 43 degrees. Your brain reads it as burning.

faq.q: Why does milk help with spicy food?
faq.a: Capsaicin is oily and doesn't mix with water. Milk contains fat and a protein called casein that help wash it away.
asks: What should I drink after eating chilli?

faq.q: Why don't birds feel chilli heat?
faq.a: Birds' heat sensors are shaped differently, so capsaicin doesn't switch them on. Birds eat chillies and spread the seeds.
With the Scoville scale. A bell pepper scores 0, a jalapeño a few thousand, and the hottest chillies over 2 million Scoville heat units.

facts: Capsaicin activates the TRPV1 receptor, which normally responds to heat above about 43 °C.
Birds are not sensitive to capsaicin and help spread chilli seeds.
